1:
Who composed the song, and when, is argued by two. Ellicott observes that the writer with his usual modesty does not claim it, yet finds it scarcely conceivable that anyone else could have written it: the piece resembles Egyptian religious poetry, with which he and probably no other Israelite of that time would have been familiar, and breathes a tone scarcely shared by any contemporary. He reports that the prophetic statements in the later verses have led some to date it after Joshua, and answers that their vagueness stands in remarkable contrast with the definiteness and graphic power of the descriptive part. Keil says the same more briefly, that though the author is not named, both contents and form put the question beyond doubt; and he sets out the structure, three gradually increasing strophes each beginning with the praise of the Lord and ending with the overthrow of the Egyptian host.

Calvin adds a different kind of argument. The song was introduced not merely in testimony of gratitude but in confirmation of the history, since it brought the hearers forward as eye-witnesses, so that later ages might know nothing had been written which had not been openly declared by six hundred thousand men besides their wives and children; and he presses the question, to whom could they have lied, when they were witnesses to one another and no stranger was listening? Henry marks the contrast with what went before, that those who had to hold their peace while the deliverance was working must not hold it now, and that the less they had to do then, the more they had to do now. Gill notes that this is the first song on record, and reports a Jewish reckoning of ten songs beginning with one sung by Adam at the forgiveness of his sins, together with another saying, not easily squared with it, that from the creation to the sea no man ever sang a song but Israel. Wesley draws a conclusion about worship, that since psalm-singing was used before the ceremonial law it is no part of that law and was not abolished with it, singing being as much the language of holy joy as praying is of holy desire.

The divine name in the second verse is remarked on by both philologists. Clarke points out that the word rendered Lord is not the full name but the contracted form, which he reports on another's authority to signify the Essence, he who is, simply and absolutely and independently. Ellicott makes the same observation about its first appearance and adds that the form was already current in speech, as an older place-name shows, and that it is chosen here for the rhythm; he notes too that a prophet afterwards took the following clause into one of his poems. On the next clause the versions divide, and Ellicott reports it: two authorities render it of preparing a habitation, while a third, the Targums, the Greek and the Latin and most moderns render it otherwise.

On the third verse Clarke and Ellicott pull in opposite directions. Clarke would change the English, preferring that the Lord is the hero of the battle, since the received phrase is now scarcely applied to anything but ships of war, and the object was to show that man had no part in the victory. Ellicott praises the translators for keeping it, calling the boldness of the anthropomorphism markedly archaic, and dismisses the ancient softenings, one making him mighty in battle and another a crusher of wars, as turgid and yet weak. Keil takes the title of one who knows how to make war and has power to destroy his foes, and reads the added name as meaning that he has just proved himself the God who rules with unlimited might. Gill refers the word for man to the future incarnation, since as yet he was not really man.
4:
Calvin explains why the narrative is told twice over. The point of the verses is simply that the drowning was manifestly God's work, and what had been plainly recounted before is now set out in more glowing terms; when the Egyptians are compared to stones and to lead, the sense is that they were hurled by God's mighty hand into the deep and had no power to swim out. Wesley catches the same force in the verb, which he says carries the sense of casting with the force of an arrow out of a bow. Clarke turns to the historical consequence: on such an expedition it is likely that the principal nobility went with their king, so that the overthrow reduced the country to the lowest extremity, and he remarks how easily Israel might have gratified itself had the people been intent on plunder or their leader moved by ambition. Ellicott corrects two small points of tense, and Gill sees in the destruction an emblem of a later overthrow of antichrist.

Ellicott alone treats the poem as a performance. He marks the end of the first strophe at the covering of the depths, where the first historical review is complete and attention has been concentrated on the single great fact of the deliverance, and he thinks it probable that at that point Miriam and her chorus of women took up the opening refrain, slightly modified, and sang it. The division agrees with the three-strophe scheme Keil had set out, but the singing of the refrain at each close is his own suggestion.

The right hand draws a philological note and a theological one. Ellicott calls it a second anthropomorphism following naturally on the first, frequent in later Scripture but here used for the first time, and corrects the tenses that follow, since the verb is a future of continuance and should be rendered that he dashes in pieces and overthrows those who rise against him and sends forth his wrath. Clarke reduces the figure to omnipotence manifested in a most extraordinary way. Keil finds the point in the timing, that the Lord overthrows his enemies at the very moment when they suppose themselves able to destroy his people. Gill refers the power to Christ and calls it the same as the Father's. On the next verse Clarke sets a prophet's later recollection beside it, where the days of old are remembered and the leading of the people by the right hand of Moses with a glorious arm, and Wesley reduces the phrase about excellency to great and excellent power.

What the blast of the nostrils is gets three answers. Clarke identifies it with the strong east wind employed to dry the sea bed, which is here represented as the breath of God that had congealed the waters so that they stood like a wall on either hand. Gill takes it the same way and explains the figure, that the wind is as easily brought by God as a man's breath is drawn through his nostrils. Wesley reads it instead of the divine anger, and glosses the congealing as the depths standing still as though frozen. On the boast that follows Keil notices the form rather than the matter, since the short clauses run on one after another without a single connecting particle, which is what conveys the enemy's confidence; Gill hears in it a man repenting that he had let the people go. On the last verse of the passage Ellicott finds something the prose narrative does not contain: a wind is here named which is additional to the earlier account though in complete harmony with it, and he suggests that as one wind had driven the waters back, a wind from the opposite quarter aided and hastened their return. Keil states the same event without the meteorology, that one breath of God was enough to sink the proud foe.
11:
The question that opens the third part is read as a controlled comparison. Clarke recalls that the plagues appear to have been directed principally against the Egyptian gods, which were thereby confounded and made despicable, so that the people are here exulting over them afresh. Ellicott says the same of the visitations, that they were meant to show the Lord exalted far above all other gods, and observes that the contrast is pressed by naming three points on which he is unapproachable, his holiness, his awefulness and his working of wonders. Calvin attends to the form rather than the matter: the song breaks into exclamation because the grandeur of the subject transcends the power of words, and the question expresses more than a plain assertion, marking both admiration and assured confidence. Wesley glosses the terms one by one, the gods being so called only and meaning idols or princes, the holiness standing for justice and mercy and truth, and the fearfulness meaning that praise must be reverent. Gill offers a rendering that would make the comparison with the mighty ones, that is, the angels; Keil marks the verse as the opening of the last strophe, where the song rises into firm assurance that the salvation begun will be finished.

How the earth came to swallow them is answered three ways. Clarke thinks it very likely that an earthquake accompanied the event, opening chasms in the sea bed which took many down, and finds the earthquake intimated in a psalm. Wesley keeps to the shore and supposes the dead bodies sank into the sands on which they were thrown and were sucked in. Ellicott sees no difficulty needing either explanation, since the sea that swallowed them is part of the earth; and he uses the case to state a principle, that if we allow our common sense fair play and permit sacred writers the same latitude as profane ones we shall find wonderfully few discrepancies.

The tense of what follows is the largest question in the passage, and each answers it differently. Clarke holds that the ode was dictated by the Spirit and that this verse and those to the end of the strophe are a prediction, so that several of the verbs would be better read as futures. Calvin grants that the Hebrew verb stands in the past but translates it as a future to make the sense clearer, since their hope for what was to come rested on mercies already received; at the next verse he repeats that he has not scrupled to change the tenses, adding that the past forms themselves confirm the certainty of the matter, a common figure with the prophets. Ellicott takes a third course and renders the verbs as presents, since Hebrew wants a present tense and lets both preterite and future carry that force, and insists that the guidance was not over but only just begun. Wesley finds a middle way, that God had put them into the way to the promised place and would in due time bring them to the end of it. Gill states plainly that all from here to the close of the song is prophecy.

The nations named are then identified. Ellicott takes the plural of the peoples to cover all the tribes of the desert and the land, points to the later histories for the fear actually felt, and notes that the inhabitants named in the second clause are the Philistines, from whom the Holy Land afterwards took its name. Clarke and Gill agree that the rulers of the next people bore a title meaning heads or chiefs rather than kings, Gill adding that a monarchy followed within a few years. Keil supplies the philology of the same words, and Calvin grounds the boast on the strength named earlier, since it was by that and not otherwise that Israel could make its way through.
17:
What mountain is meant divides them. Clarke offers Canaan, a very mountainous country, or probably the hill on which the temple was afterwards built. Ellicott reports the view that one particular hill is intended and prefers the land at large, which consists almost entirely of mountains and has only two plains of any extent; the sanctuary, he says, can only mean the place where God was to put his name, and is spoken of as though already prepared. Calvin explains the figure of planting as denoting a firm habitation, and finds a motive in the mention of the sanctuary, since by that commendation the desire of the land is excited in hearts otherwise indifferent. Wesley argues that if God brought them out of Egypt he will bring them into Canaan, for having begun will he not make an end; and adds that it is good dwelling where God dwells, in his church on earth and in heaven. Gill notes that the bringing in is ascribed to the Lord as much as the bringing out; Keil renders the whole as future.

The closing line is taken as a chorus. Clarke calls it the grand chorus in which all the people joined, expressing dominion not only in the world but in the Church, not only under the law but under the Gospel, not only in time but through eternity, and offers a rendering of the phrase as for ever and onward. Ellicott judges that in simplicity, and in the force that comes of it, this expression of the idea transcends all later ones. Gill refers the reign to Christ, dating its beginning in eternity.

Whether the verse that follows belongs to the song is doubted by two and left open by a third. Ellicott states flatly that it is parenthetic and forms no part of the poem, and accounts for it thus: when the song was still a separate document the verse was appended as an historical comment showing the occasion of its composition, and when the records were gathered up the addition was kept although by then unnecessary. Calvin reaches the same judgment on internal grounds, that the verse is unsuited to the song, and concludes that the writer here returns to the history to assign the reason why the people celebrated God's praises so magnificently; to avoid ambiguity he would render the verbs as pluperfects. Gill leaves open whether the words conclude the song by recapitulation or resume the narrative; Keil takes the singular horse to mean Pharaoh riding at the head of his army.

Miriam's part is described three ways, and Ellicott fastens on her standing. In her, he says, we have the first of that long series of religious women in Scripture who are not merely pious but exercise a quasi-ministerial office; he lists the later prophetesses and adds that the early Church had an order of deaconesses. Calvin explains the arrangement from the practice of the lyric poets, calling this the antistrophe: God would have not only men proclaim the miracle but associated the women with them, so that when the men had finished the women followed in order. Wesley describes two assemblies, one leader giving out the psalm for the men and the other for the women, with timbrels and dances after the usage of those times, and recalls that famous victories were commonly applauded by the daughters of Israel. Gill notes that the word for answering is masculine and that the women repeated the same song word for word after the men. Clarke works out that she was older than either brother, since she was a girl able to manage the stratagem at the river when the younger was exposed and the elder was then barely three; and Gill reports that her name, the same as Mary, signifies bitterness, derived by the Hebrews from the bitterness of the times in which she was born.
22:
That the people had to be brought away from the shore at all is taken as significant. Gill reports two suppositions, that they were unwilling to leave because they were intent on the spoil cast up on the beach, whose harness a rabbinic authority describes as ornamented with gold and silver and precious stones, or that they had a mind to turn back and take Egypt for themselves, its military force being destroyed and its armour now in their hands; but he prefers the plain sense, that their general gave the word to march and until then they stayed. Henry adopts the difficulty and adds a third cause, that they were taken up with the sight or with the song or with the stripping of the dead bodies and did not care to go forward, and he draws the lesson that the pleasures of the way to Canaan must not retard our progress but quicken it, though a wilderness lies ahead. Ellicott corrects the connecting word and marks the resumption of the narrative, noting that the people are now carried two stages towards the mountain.

Ellicott then does what none of the others attempt and fixes the ground. It is uncertain at what point of the coast they came out of the sea-bed, but it can scarcely have been far from the modern port; and the springs some seven miles from it, where there is considerable vegetation and a number of wells reckoned by different travellers at seven, seventeen and nineteen, may well have been the halting-place at which the song was composed and sung. Clarke places the wilderness they entered on the coast, on the road to the mountain, and Henry marks the trial in it, that a want of water was a sore thing for young travellers and a diminution of their joy, by which God would train them up to difficulties.

Calvin weighs the complaint carefully and finds it inexcusable. Three days of thirst in a dry land, with no relief anywhere and the first water discovered bitter, was no light temptation, and it is no wonder they groaned with anxiety; but grief that is full of contumacy deserves no pardon. In such an emergency they should have turned their prayers to God, whereas they not only neglected to pray but violently assailed their leader and demanded of him the drink they knew that God alone could give. Clarke is gentler with them, ascribing the murmuring to a state of great mental degradation brought on by long and oppressive bondage, which had left them without firmness of character; and Gill states the grievance simply, that they had been brought into a wilderness where they could find no water fit to drink.

The place itself is described by the travellers. Ellicott says the extreme bitterness of the springs at that end of the wilderness is attested by every traveller, naming three, and that of the several such springs the most copious is scarcely the bitterest of them; he adds that the name means bitterness in both Hebrew and Arabic and appears to be a form of the root that gives the Latin words for the sea and for what is bitter. Clarke reports another traveller's conjecture identifying the site with a place where a small rill still runs brackish unless diluted by dew or rain. Wesley gives the name in three words. Keil turns to what was done there, that when the cry went up God showed a wood which took the bitterness away when thrown in, and observes that the Bedouins who know the country are acquainted with no such tree and with no other means of sweetening bitter water.
25:
Clarke observes that Moses was not only their leader but also their mediator. On the tree he reports that some think it was extremely bitter in itself, such as the quassia, and that God acted here as he generally does, correcting contraries by contraries, a favourite maxim among ancient physicians. Ellicott takes a more careful position. There are trees which can sweeten bitter water, but none is at present found in the peninsula, and perhaps in ancient times there were forms of vegetable life there which do not now exist; Moses would scarcely have been shown a tree unless the tree had some virtue of its own, but on the other hand the tree alone is scarcely to be credited with the entire effect. Calvin marks that Moses alone duly prayed while the people rose tumultuously against him, and that God might have given them sweet water to drink at first, but wished by the bitter to make prominent the bitterness which lurked in their hearts. Wesley draws the practical use, that it is the greatest relief of the cares of magistrates and ministers, when those under their charge make them uneasy, that they may have recourse to God by prayer, for he is the guide of the church's guides; and God is to be acknowledged not only in creating things useful for man but in discovering their usefulness. Gill says shortly that it is a happy thing to have a God to go to in trouble.

The statute and ordinance made there are read three ways. Clarke holds that the following verse is precisely what is intended by them, unfolding it into the acknowledgment of Jehovah alone with the avoidance of idolatry and the reception of his word and testimony as a divine revelation. Calvin denies that the reference is to the whole law afterwards given on Sinai and makes it a special admonition, that if the Israelites were tractable and obedient God on his part would be kind and bountiful, with an implied rebuke that their troubles are brought on by their own sins, the Egyptians being the standing example of what he does to those who resist him. Gill reads it as preparation, that a people so lately delivered from bondage were now to expect a body of laws, not being without law to God.

At the last stage the commentators turn topographical. Gill dates the arrival to the twenty-fifth of the month, notes on the authority of Aben Ezra that they stayed only one day at the bitter waters, and cites two placements of the camp, one on the northern skirts of the desert, the other eight miles from the previous station; the twelve wells and seventy palms he takes at face value as plenty of water and shady trees, the fruit not being ripe at that season. Clarke reports the Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem, which make it one well for each tribe and one palm for each of the seventy elders, and against that sets a traveller who found nine of the twelve wells, the other three choked with sand, and the palms multiplied into more than two thousand, whose dates bring a considerable revenue to the Greek monks of the neighbouring port. Ellicott identifies the place with a particular valley, where abundant grass grows thick and high and acacias and tamarisks are plentiful, and where, despite the ruthless denudation of the country by the Arabs, a certain number of palm-trees remain, though not seventy and either dwarf, that is trunkless, or stunted. Keil says only that it has been sought from olden time in that same valley, about six miles south of the bitter spring.

Calvin alone asks what the station meant. A more pleasant place was granted to the people; but we learn from what precedes that this was a concession to their infirmity, because they had borne their thirst so impatiently.
